## What you just did, as diagrams
:::

```{=html}
<div id="f7-explain" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<!-- f7-explain:start (written from the data file by the test's --write mode; do not edit) -->
<dl class="lx-ideas"><dt>A microgrid</dt><dd>Loads and sources inside one boundary, run as one unit by a controller, that can island: open its switch and run on its own.</dd><dt>Forming an island</dt><dd>A <span class="lx-term" data-term="grid-forming">grid-forming</span> source, such as a battery's <span class="lx-term" data-term="inverter">inverter</span> or a generator, sets <span class="lx-term" data-term="voltage">voltage</span> and <span class="lx-term" data-term="frequency">frequency</span>; ordinary solar inverters follow it.</dd><dt>Power, then energy</dt><dd>Power (kW) decides which loads the island can carry at once; stored energy and fuel (kWh) decide for how long.</dd><dt>Seasons</dt><dd>The same campus kept 650 kW for 20 hours in July and 8 in January: weaker sun leaves more of the load to the generator and battery, so their energy runs out sooner.</dd><dt>No grid at all</dt><dd>A village <span class="lx-term" data-term="mini-grid">mini-grid</span> runs as an island every day; running big loads while the sun shines keeps its battery small.</dd></dl><p class="lx-eyebrow">The parts of a microgrid</p><ol class="f7-notes"><li><b>Grid feeder.</b> The utility's distribution line that brings grid power to the campus.</li><li><b>Switch to the grid.</b> The <span class="lx-term" data-term="point-of-common-coupling">point of common coupling</span>: the one place the campus meets the grid. Opening it islands the campus.</li><li><b>Controller.</b> Decides when to island, which sources run and which loads stay on.</li><li><b>Solar panels, 600 kW.</b> Their <span class="lx-term" data-term="inverter">inverters</span> are <span class="lx-term" data-term="grid-following">grid-following</span>: they follow a voltage that something else sets, so they cannot start an island alone.</li><li><b>Battery, 500 kW and 2,000 kWh.</b> Its <span class="lx-term" data-term="grid-forming">grid-forming</span> inverter can set the island's voltage and frequency at once.</li><li><b>Diesel generator, 400 kW.</b> Fuel for 24 hours at full power. Once started, it can form an island too.</li><li><b>County hospital, 300 kW.</b> <span class="lx-term" data-term="critical-load">Critical load</span>: it must stay on.</li><li><b>Water and heating plant, 100 kW.</b> Critical too: the hospital needs water and heat.</li><li><b>Dorms, 250 kW.</b> Can go dark in an emergency, if they must.</li><li><b>Classrooms and labs, 550 kW.</b> The largest load, and the first to shed.</li></ol><p class="lx-eyebrow">Kinds of microgrid</p><div class="lx-scroll-x"><table class="lx-mini-table f7-fb"><caption class="lx-hint">The first four rows follow DOE's microgrid overview (2019); the village row follows the World Bank's 2025 energy-access report.</caption><thead><tr><th scope="col">Kind</th><th scope="col">What it is for</th><th scope="col">Grid link</th><th scope="col">In this lesson</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr><td>Commercial or industrial</td><td>Cut costs while connected; backup power in an outage</td><td>Connected, can island</td><td>–</td></tr><tr><td>Community, city or utility</td><td>Reliability, emissions and energy goals</td><td>Connected, can island</td><td>–</td></tr><tr><td>Facility, such as a campus</td><td>Link critical facilities and their equipment</td><td>Connected, can island</td><td>Prairie Campus</td></tr><tr><td>Rural community or island</td><td>Burn less imported fuel; more resilience</td><td>Sometimes connected</td><td>–</td></tr><tr><td>Village mini-grid</td><td>Electricity where no grid reaches</td><td>None</td><td>The village</td></tr></tbody></table></div>
<!-- f7-explain:end -->
</div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Analyst</span>Does the microgrid pay off?</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

- Keeping the same loads on for longer may need more storage or fuel: a bigger battery, a bigger tank.
- Whether that pays depends on what an hour without power costs the hospital, a farm or a household. Analyst lesson [A14](a14-microgrid-value.html) prices an outage and sizes the campus against it.
- Who owns the microgrid decides who pays for it and who carries the risk: a utility, a co-op, the county or a private company.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Modeler</span>Letting a solver size and run it</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

- This lesson runs the island by one fixed rule: generator first, then the battery. It is a rule, not the best way.
- A sizing model makes each size a [decision variable]{.lx-term term="decision-variable"} and writes every hour's balance, and each outage, as rules; [lesson 10](10-write-it-down.html) writes a small model like this down.
- Modeler lesson [M5](m05-microgrid-size-and-run.html) sizes a microgrid that must survive an outage, with on/off decisions solved as in [lesson 11](11-solver.html).

## Check yourself
:::

```{=html}
<p class="lx-lede">Practice, about 10 minutes: three myths, two questions, then sort six systems.</p>
<div class="lx-myths" data-quiz="f7-myth">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="rooftop" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “My rooftop solar keeps my lights on in a blackout.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth, for an ordinary grid-connected system: under IEEE 1547-2018 its inverter stops feeding an unintentional island, normally within 2 seconds. Backup needs a switch that isolates the home and equipment that can island; a battery keeps it going without sunshine.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="generator" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A microgrid is just a big backup generator.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. A microgrid runs loads and sources inside one boundary as one unit, with a controller and a switch to the grid; it can serve one building or many. A generator alone, with no controller or local network, is backup.</p></details>
</div>
<!-- f7-myth:start (written from the model by the test's --write mode; do not edit) -->
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="double" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “Doubling the battery doubles how long the hospital stays lit.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. Keeping the hospital and the water plant from midnight on 28 July 2025, 2,000 kWh lasts 51 hours and 4,000 kWh lasts 67: the fuel and the sun set the rest.</p></details>
</div>
<!-- f7-myth:end -->
</div>

<div class="lx-quiz" data-quiz="f7">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="hours" data-answer="b">
<p class="lx-qtext">A battery holds 2,000 kWh and can give 500 kW. The hospital and the water plant draw 400 kW, with no sun and no generator. How long does the battery carry them?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">4 hours</li><li data-value="b">5 hours</li><li data-value="c">8 hours</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>5 hours: 2,000 kWh ÷ 400 kW. The 400 kW fits under the battery's 500 kW, so its energy is the limit.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="power" data-answer="a">
<p class="lx-qtext">Same battery, still no sun or generator, but the labs stay on too: 950 kW. What stops the island?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">Power: 950 kW is more than the battery's 500 kW</li><li data-value="b">Energy: 2,000 kWh runs out</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Power. The battery cannot give more than 500 kW at once, so the island falls short at once, long before its 2,000 kWh run out.</p></details>
</div>
</div>

<div id="f7-sort" class="lx-card">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">Microgrid or not? Sort six systems</p>
<div class="lx-fallback">
<!-- f7-sort:start (written from the data file by the test's --write mode; do not edit) -->
<ul><li>A campus with solar, a battery, a generator, a controller and one switch to the grid</li><li>A village's panels, batteries and wires, with no grid connection at all</li><li>A house with rooftop solar and an ordinary grid-connected inverter</li><li>A standby generator on its own, with no controller, that starts after the grid fails</li><li>A wind farm connected to the transmission grid</li><li>An island's diesel generators, wind turbines and batteries, with no link to a mainland</li></ul><details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answers</summary><ul><li><b>A microgrid:</b> a campus with solar, a battery, a generator, a controller and one switch to the grid. Loads and sources inside one boundary, run as one unit, and able to island.</li><li><b>A microgrid:</b> a village's panels, batteries and wires, with no grid connection at all. An isolated microgrid: it runs as an island all the time.</li><li><b>Not a microgrid:</b> a house with rooftop solar and an ordinary grid-connected inverter. It cannot run alone: its inverter stops when the grid does.</li><li><b>Not a microgrid:</b> a standby generator on its own, with no controller, that starts after the grid fails. Backup, not a microgrid: no controller runs sources and loads as one unit. A microgrid can still serve a single building.</li><li><b>Not a microgrid:</b> a wind farm connected to the transmission grid. A power plant that sells to the grid; it serves no local loads of its own.</li><li><b>A microgrid:</b> an island's diesel generators, wind turbines and batteries, with no link to a mainland. A whole small grid run as one unit, isolated from any larger one.</li></ul></details>
<!-- f7-sort:end -->
</div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<tr><td class="n">461 · 3.1 GW</td><td>Operating U.S. microgrids in DOE's Microgrid Installation Database when it launched, and their total capacity.</td><td class="s"><a href="https://www.energy.gov/cmei/ito/articles/department-energy-releases-new-tool-tracking-microgrid-installations-united">U.S. DOE</a> · 26 May 2021</td></tr>
<tr><td class="n">over 666 million</td><td>People without electricity in 2023. Mini-grids and off-grid solar are among the ways to reach them.</td><td class="s"><a href="https://www.worldbank.org/en/news/press-release/2025/06/25/energy-access-has-improved-yet-international-financial-support-still-needed-to-boost-progress-and-address-disparities">World Bank, Tracking SDG 7 (2025)</a> · 25 June 2025</td></tr>
<tr><td class="n">2 s</td><td>How fast an ordinary grid-connected inverter must normally detect an unintentional island and stop feeding it; up to 5 s by agreement with the utility.</td><td class="s"><a href="https://doi.org/10.1109/IEEESTD.2018.8332112">IEEE Std 1547-2018</a> · published April 2018</td></tr>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-card lx-real">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">In the real world</p>
<p>In Puerto Rico, a small microgrid that serves a community organization kept the power on for nine days during Hurricane Fiona, while other parts of the island were dark (<a href="https://www.energy.gov/cmei/articles/success-story-new-tool-connects-multiple-microgrids-increase-community-resilience">U.S. DOE, 8 November 2023</a>).</p>
<blockquote class="lx-excerpt" data-source="excerpt:campus-resilience-question"><p>In an industry internship, the course author worked on this question: how should solar <span class="lx-term" data-term="photovoltaic">PV</span>, battery storage and backup generation be sized for an industrial campus to meet demand through grid outages?</p><p>The work used a <span class="lx-term" data-term="techno-economic-optimization">techno-economic optimization</span> model to size a resilient microgrid for the campus.</p><p>The company's data, models and results are confidential and are not shown here.</p></blockquote>
<blockquote class="lx-excerpt" data-source="excerpt:supply-chain-mg"><p>From the course author's research: in the modeled supply chains, each open factory or warehouse could run its own microgrid, with on-site wind, solar and storage, an energy balance every hour, and energy bought from and sold to the grid.</p><footer>Approved excerpt of: Li et al. (2023), <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.apm.2023.02.014">Applied Mathematical Modelling</a>.</footer></blockquote>
<ul class="lx-hint f7-holds"><li>Holds when: <span class="lx-term" data-term="stylized-network">stylized networks</span> with synthetic distances and costs, candidate sites in California, Arizona and Nevada, and one year, planned week by week for products and hour by hour for energy.</li><li>Leaves out: grid outages, which the studies do not model.</li></ul>
<p class="lx-hint">The full case: <a href="cf1-supply-chain-microgrids.html">case file CF1</a>.</p>
</div>
<div class="lx-card lx-sources">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">Sources and further reading</p>
```
